title: What AI Can Learn From James Gleick's The Telephone Book
summary: James Gleick's The Telephone explores how technologies shape users while being shaped by them, offering crucial lessons for AI development in 2026.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- James Gleick's new book traces telephone history from the 1870s to 1984, revealing how technologies evolve unpredictably through user adoption.
- The book draws striking parallels between telephone adoption patterns and today's AI transformation, from uncertain use cases to emerging social norms.
- Gleick's historical analysis suggests AI builders won't control how their technology ultimately reshapes society, just as Bell couldn't envision modern telecommunications.


James Gleick's latest work, The Telephone: A New History, officially released on November 1, 2026, arrives at a moment when society grapples with artificial intelligence's rapid transformation of daily life. The book's central thesis, that important technologies arrive unformed and then shape their users while being shaped by them, offers a crucial framework for understanding AI's current trajectory.


## The Unpredictable Birth of Transformative Technology


Gleick traces telephony's development through the stories of pioneering tinkerers in the 1870s, culminating in the famous patent race between Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray. On Valentine's Day 1876, both filed telephone-related applications. Bell's wealthy patrons allegedly reached a corrupt patent officer first, securing what became one of history's most valuable pieces of intellectual property. Gray lost out and held a justifiable grudge for life.


The immediate uncertainty about what phones would actually be for mirrors today's AI debates. Early proponents envisioned phones primarily for mass distribution of musical performances, religious sermons, and government propaganda. Thomas Edison dismissed the device as good for nothing but "conversational chitchat." The parallel to current disagreements about whether AI constitutes an alien mind or merely powerful productivity software is striking.


## Phone Doomers and Social Norms


Edwin Butler, editor of Illinois's Stark County News, predicted phones would make people lazier, undercut privacy, and "multiply a million times the power of human gab and deluge the world with talk." He warned everyone would eventually put phones by their beds, fraying nerves by consuming news and gossip around the clock. This 19th-century hand-wringing reads as both quaint and prescient today.


Gleick writes engagingly about how social mores evolved organically. AT&T published educational materials explaining basics like how long to let a phone ring (8 to 10 times) and what to say when answering. Yet these instructions proved unnecessary. People created norms simply by calling each other, demonstrating how users, not inventors, ultimately define technology's social role.


## Legal Frameworks and Innovation Constraints


As one legal scholar notes in the book, "it was the lawyers, as much as anyone else, who invented the telephone." Bell's patent gave rise to the monopolistic Bell System, through which AT&T decided what would work best for its purposes. Its legal department forced everyone else to live with those decisions, down to what phones in homes could look like.


This iron grip didn't prevent innovation entirely. Gleick presents the telephone era as prehistory for the internet, describing how advances in telephone switching laid groundwork for transistors that would power computers and networking. Phone users developed an appetite for conversational chitchat that eventually evolved into the World Wide Web's hive mind.


## Release Date and Modern Relevance


The Telephone officially launched on November 1, 2026, though its narrative concludes on January 1, 1984, when decades of antitrust litigation dismantled the Bell System monopoly. Gleick notes this monumental business change came exactly one year after the US government's Arpanet transitioned to the communications standard enabling the modern internet. These technological and legal shifts laid groundwork for the iPhone and everything following.


While a smartphone appears on the cover, the book treats the iPhone age as afterthought. Its real focus remains the formative century when telephone technology and social practices co-evolved in ways no single inventor could have predicted or controlled.


## What This Means for AI Development


Less than four years after ChatGPT's introduction, we appear in the early stages of another monumental technological shift. Fundamental disagreements persist among AI builders about what the technology even is. Cultural norms about AI use are only beginning to emerge painfully. People who should be developing legal frameworks have not shown they're remotely up to the challenge.


Describing the telephone-created world, Gleick writes it's one Bell "could never have envisioned and would not have liked." If people write books 100 years from now, the same will likely be said about AI. But as The Telephone illustrates through meticulous historical analysis, inventors don't really get to decide how their creations reshape civilization. Users do.
